<explanation>
Based on the file tree and README content, this project is Dex – a federated OpenID Connect provider that manages authentication flows and acts as a proxy for external identity providers via “connectors”. The goal of your diagram is to present an accurate, high-level view of Dex’s architecture while capturing its modular components and the way they interact.

Below is a step-by-step guide to drawing an effective system design diagram for Dex:

1. Identify the Main Components:
   • External Clients: Represent the user-facing applications (such as web browsers, mobile apps, or other services) that authenticate using OpenID Connect. Label these as “Client Applications” or “OAuth2 / OIDC Clients.”
   • Dex Core Service: This is the central component composed of the “cmd/dex” and “server” packages. It handles authentication flows, token issuance (ID tokens, refresh tokens), and acts as the gateway between clients and connectors.
   • Web Interface: Depicted by the “web” directory, this component includes static assets (templates, CSS, images) and builds the user login and approval UI.
   • Connectors Layer: Represented by the “connector” directory, which contains multiple submodules (LDAP, GitHub, SAML, etc.). These modules act as adapters to external identity providers. Indicate that each connector supports different protocols and features.
   • Storage Backend: Show various storage modules from the “storage” directory (SQL, memory, etc.) that persist tokens, client configs, and session data. Note that Dex supports multiple storage options and uses configuration-driven strategies.
   • API & Protobuf Interfaces: The “api” (and “api/v2”) directories contain protocol definitions (via protobuf) and gRPC services. These can be represented as a communication layer for programmatic interaction (e.g., between components or with clients that prefer gRPC).
   • Configuration / Deployment: Additional files – like configuration YAML files, Docker Compose, Dockerfile, and Kubernetes manifests – indicate how Dex is deployed and configured. Optionally include a “Deployment/Config” cluster block to capture environment specifics.

2. Define Relationships and Data Flow:
   • Draw arrows from the “External Clients” to the “Web Interface” and/or “Dex Core Service” to depict login requests using OAuth2/OpenID Connect.
   • From the “Dex Core Service,” illustrate connections to the “Connectors Layer” which in turn communicate with external identity providers (e.g., LDAP, GitHub, SAML, etc.).
   • Include bidirectional arrows between the Dex core and the “Storage” modules to show persistence operations (reading/writing tokens, client details, sessions).
   • If you include the API layer, use arrows that denote how the service uses gRPC endpoints defined in the “api” folders.
   • Optionally, illustrate the configuration/deployment layer and how it surrounds all components (for example, Dex running as a container managed by Kubernetes).

3. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   • Modular Design: Emphasize how Dex is organized into distinct packages that separate concerns (authentication logic, connectors, storage, API, and web presentation). 
   • Plugin-like Connector Architecture: Show that connectors are loosely coupled modules that can be added or removed based on operator configuration.
   • Configuration-Driven: Note the use of YAML-based configuration files and environment variables (.envrc, config.yaml.dist) that control which connectors are enabled and tuning settings.
   • Cloud Native & Containerization: Mention support for Kubernetes (with manifests and CRDs) and use of Docker for containerization.

4. Include Specific Technologies and Frameworks:
   • Language: Emphasize that the system is written in Go.
   • Protocols: Include OpenID Connect, OAuth2 flows, and gRPC communication (via protobuf API definitions).
   • Infrastructure: Reference Docker, Kubernetes, and Continuous Integration (evidenced by GitHub workflows and Docker Compose files).

5. Diagram Customization for Dex’s Specifics:
   • Clearly separate the external-facing layers (client interactions via the web login and API endpoints) from the internal processing layers (Dex core, connectors, storage).
   • Use different shapes or colors to differentiate between types of components. For example, use rectangles for core services, cylinders for storage/database layers, and rounded rectangles or icons for external identity providers.
   • Include directional arrows to showcase the authentication flow:
       - Client initiates authentication → Web UI (login page)
       - Web UI forwards the request to Dex Core
       - Dex Core invokes the appropriate Connector module to delegate authentication to the identity provider
       - Results and tokens flow back from the Connector to the Dex Core, which in turn generates an ID Token that is sent back to the client.
   • Optionally incorporate a legend to indicate what each shape or color represents.

6. Finalizing the Diagram:
   • Label each component clearly (e.g., “Dex API / Core Service”, “Connector – GitHub”, “Storage – SQL / Memory”, “Web UI”).
   • Ensure directional arrows indicate data flow/dependencies and that you show how external systems (identity providers) interact with the “Connectors” module.
   • Verify that the diagram captures both the high-level flow of authentication and the inter-module interactions (e.g., configuration, token exchange, and persistence operations).

By capturing these aspects, the diagram will effectively communicate Dex’s architecture to engineers, offering clarity on the separation of concerns, data flows, and how the system integrates with various external identity providers. Remember to keep the diagram detailed enough to be useful, yet sufficiently abstract so that it conveys the overall structure and modular design of the system.
</explanation>
